newsitem.title: UK: POLL-UK RETAIL PRICES TO STAY ABOVE TARGET IN JULY.
newsitem.headline: POLL-UK RETAIL PRICES TO STAY ABOVE TARGET IN JULY.

text.p: Annual British retail price inflation is expected to have crept up in July, pushing the underlying rate further above the government target of 2.5 percent, according to a Reuter poll of economists.
The poll produced a consensus forecast that RPIX, which measures retail prices excluding volatile home loan payments, rose 2.8 percent in the year to July, up from 2.7 in June.
The headline inflation rate is expected to break above three percent, to 3.1, for the first time since end-1995.
But much of that can be ascribed to rising mortgage rates, forced up by a flurry of official interest rate rises. The figures are due at 0830 GMT on Tuesday.
Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said mortgage rate rises would push headline RPI up to 3.2 percent year-on-year.

The Bank of England, now free to set monetary policy in its quest to keep underlying inflation at 2.5 percent, has pushed base rates up to seven percent in four quarter-point moves since the Labour Party's landslide election victory on May 1.
More pressure will come from rising petrol prices, following duty increases introduced by Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown in his July 2 budget, and buoyant seasonal food prices.

"The main upwards pressure on RPI this month stems from petrol prices, which we estimate rose by three percent following the budget, and seasonal food prices, which are expected to have fallen by less than last year," Barr said.

Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers, said the budget increase in petrol duty would add 0.3 percent to prices, while seasonal food prices would have a downward influence on inflation in the month but an upward one on the yearly rate.
"Seasonal food prices rose sharply in June this year and we expect that they will fall in July but show a smaller decline than last year's unusually weak figure," he said.
Traditionally, retail price data represent the key economic news for British markets and this month will be no exception.
But since the Bank of England's monetary policy committee raised base rates again last week and hinted that was the last move for a while, economists said market reaction might be muted.
The Bank said its committee now thought interest rates had reached a level consistent with the inflation target being met in two years' time.

Saunders said a flood of windfall payments from building society flotations -- about 35 billion pounds in free shares have been handed out -- and higher indirect taxes following Brown's first budget would lift inflation in the near term.
"But the recent rate hikes, plus the drag from the high pound, will cap UK growth late this year or in early 1998," he said.

As a result, he said the Bank's quarterly inflation report, to be released on Wednesday, was likely to project that inflation would be close to target in two years' time if base rates stick at seven percent.
